points.heading: 1. Educational & Awareness Purpose Only
points.text: Nyaya Mitra is an open-source civic initiative designed solely for legal awareness and informational reference. It does not constitute formal legal counsel, attorney-client representation, or professional legal advice.

points.heading: 2. Statutory Basis & Dynamic Application
points.text: All information is referenced from the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, the Constitution of India, and landmark Supreme Court judgments. However, legal outcomes and procedures vary based on specific facts, jurisdictions, and evidence.

points.heading: 3. State-Specific Variations
points.text: Police Complaints Authority (PCA) mechanisms, vigilance reporting lines, and local traffic e-challan systems vary by state and union territory. Always consult state-specific portals where applicable.

points.heading: 4. Emergency Situations
points.text: In any situation involving imminent physical threat, violence, or immediate danger, prioritize your physical safety and immediately contact the National Emergency Support System at 112 or NALSA Free Legal Aid at 15100.

scenarios.title: Pulled Over / Traffic Stop
scenarios.quickSummary: Police must be in uniform with a visible name badge. They cannot snatch your car keys or search your mobile phone without legal cause.
panicSteps: Ask politely for the officer's name, badge number, and police station.
Present your driving license and RC via DigiLocker or mParivahan (Rule 139 CMVR).
Do not surrender your phone for search and demand a printed e-Challan receipt if fined.
yourRights: An officer below Sub-Inspector (SI) rank cannot issue fines for major offenses (must have uniform badge/stars).
You are legally entitled to present digital documents via DigiLocker or mParivahan (Rule 139 CMVR / IT Act Sec. 4).
Traffic police cannot forcibly remove your ignition key or deflate your tires.
You cannot be compelled to surrender your phone for search during a routine document check.

dos: Politely ask for the officer's name, badge number, and designated police station.
Present driving license and RC through DigiLocker or mParivahan apps.
Always demand an official printed e-Challan receipt if fined; verify transaction ID.
donts: Never hand over unreceipted physical cash under the pretext of an on-the-spot settlement.
Do not engage in physical altercations or resist lawful document verification.

whereToComplain.action: Lodge online challan dispute citing the officer badge number and timestamp.
File a formal written complaint against high-handed behavior or unlawful vehicle impoundment.

citations.description: Mandates recognition of digital documents via DigiLocker/mParivahan.
Governs reasonable grounds for questioning without arbitrary restraint.

scenarios.title: Arrest & Detention Safeguards
scenarios.quickSummary: You have constitutional protections against arbitrary detention, right to legal counsel, and immediate family notification.
panicSteps: Ask immediately: 'What are the grounds of arrest, and is this offense bailable?' (BNSS §47).
Demand a signed Arrest Memo and name a family member/friend who must be informed (BNSS §48).
Call NALSA 15100 for free legal aid or contact your lawyer immediately (Art. 22).
yourRights: Right to know the exact grounds of arrest immediately upon detention (Art. 22(1)).
Right to an Arrest Memo stating date, time, location, signed by an independent local witness and the arresting officer (D.K. Basu Guidelines).
Right to inform one family member or friend within 8–12 hours of arrest (BNSS Sec. 48 / CrPC Sec. 50A).
Mandatory production before the nearest Judicial Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest (Art. 22(2)).
Right to free legal aid from DLSA if unrepresented (Art. 39A).

dos: Demand to see the signed Arrest Memo and ensure a copy is given to you or your family.
Request an immediate medical examination at a government hospital upon arrest and every 48 hours during custody.
Exercise your statutory right to place a phone call to your family or lawyer.
donts: Never sign blank papers, unsigned statements, or coerced confessions under pressure.
Do not physically resist arrest, as it can invite additional charges under BNS Sec. 221.

whereToComplain.action: Directly inform the magistrate during first appearance of any custodial mistreatment or denial of memo.
Submit petition for unlawful custody beyond 24 hours or custodial violence.

citations.description: Fundamental right to life, legal representation, and 24-hour magistrate production.

citations.section: D.K. Basu v. State of WB (1997)
citations.description: 11 mandatory guidelines for arrest, detention, and custodial safeguards.
Mandatory disclosure of arrest grounds and family notification.

scenarios.title: Rights of Women During Arrest
scenarios.quickSummary: Women cannot be arrested between sunset and sunrise except under exceptional circumstances with prior Magistrate permission.
panicSteps: Demand a female police officer for any physical search or custody (BNSS §51).
Refuse arrest between 6 PM (sunset) and 6 AM (sunrise) without a written Magistrate order (BNSS §43(5)).
Insist that questioning takes place at your residence if summoned as a witness (BNSS §179).
yourRights: No woman can be arrested after sunset (6 PM) and before sunrise (6 AM) without prior written permission from a Judicial Magistrate (BNSS Sec. 43(5) / CrPC Sec. 46(4)).
Only a female police officer can search or physically touch a woman (BNSS Sec. 51 / CrPC Sec. 51(2)).
A woman witness cannot be summoned to a police station; interrogation must take place at her residence (BNSS Sec. 179 / CrPC Sec. 160).

dos: Demand the presence of a female officer before permitting any physical search or custody.
Refuse overnight detention at a police station without a written judicial magistrate warrant.
Insist that a family member or legal counsel remains present during questioning.
donts: Do not accompany male police personnel alone after dark.

whereToComplain.action: Direct escalation for unlawful arrest, harassment, or custodial misconduct.
Lodge formal grievance for violation of constitutional dignity and procedural protocols.

citations.description: Sunset-to-sunrise arrest prohibition and mandatory female search protocols.

citations.section: Sheela Barse v. State of Maharashtra (1983)
citations.description: Mandates separate female lockups and protection against custodial harassment.

scenarios.title: Police Refusing to Register FIR
scenarios.quickSummary: Police are legally mandated to register an FIR for cognizable offenses immediately without delay.
panicSteps: Ask the officer to record the complaint in the General Diary (GD) and provide the GD Entry Number.
Demand a 'Zero FIR' if jurisdiction is cited as an excuse to turn you away.
Send the signed complaint via Registered Speed Post / Email to the SP/DCP under BNSS §173(3).
yourRights: Mandatory registration: Police cannot refuse to register an FIR if a cognizable offense (theft, assault, robbery, fraud) is disclosed (Lalita Kumari ruling).
Zero FIR: You can file an FIR at ANY police station regardless of where the crime occurred; the station must transfer it to the jurisdictional station.
Right to a free copy: You are entitled to an immediate, stamped copy of the FIR at zero cost (BNSS Sec. 173(2) / CrPC Sec. 154(2)).

dos: Request the Station House Officer (SHO) to record your complaint in the General Diary (GD) and provide the GD Entry Number.
Insist on registering a 'Zero FIR' if jurisdiction is cited as an excuse.
Send the signed complaint via Registered Post / Speed Post / Email to the Superintendent of Police (SP) or DCP.
donts: Do not leave the station without either an FIR copy or a stamped receipt/GD acknowledgment.

whereToComplain.action: Submit written complaint under BNSS Sec. 173(3) / CrPC Sec. 154(3); the SP must investigate or direct FIR registration.
File an application under BNSS Sec. 175(3) / CrPC Sec. 156(3) seeking court orders to direct police to register FIR.

citations.section: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of UP (2014)
citations.description: FIR registration is mandatory upon receipt of cognizable offense information.
Governs procedure for FIR registration and escalation to Superintendent of Police.

scenarios.title: Search & Seizure of Property
scenarios.quickSummary: Searches of home or vehicle require a valid warrant or strict compliance with independent witness requirements.
panicSteps: Ask to inspect the written Search Warrant and verify the Magistrate's seal.
Insist that two independent local witnesses (Panchas) are present throughout the search (BNSS §103).
Demand a signed inventory list (Seizure Memo / Panchnama) before anything leaves your premises.
yourRights: Police require a valid Search Warrant issued by a Magistrate, except in hot pursuit or urgent investigation of cognizable crimes.
Searches must be conducted in the presence of two independent and respectable inhabitants of the locality (Panchas) (BNSS Sec. 103 / CrPC Sec. 100).
You have the right to receive a signed copy of the Seizure Memo (Panchnama) listing all confiscated items.
Occupants must be permitted to be present during the search.

dos: Ask to inspect the written Search Warrant and verify the magistrate's seal and officer's name.
Insist that two local neighbors or independent witnesses are present throughout the search.
Demand a comprehensive written list of seized articles signed by the witnesses before anything leaves the premises.
donts: Do not permit an unrecorded search or surrender items without a formal written receipt.

whereToComplain.action: File an application challenging illegal seizure under BNSS Sec. 503 / CrPC Sec. 451/457 for return of property.
Report arbitrary house trespassing or unauthorized seizure of personal devices.

citations.description: Search procedures, Panch witness mandates, and inventory list generation.

scenarios.title: Police Demanding Bribes / Extortion
scenarios.quickSummary: Demanding or accepting illegal gratification is a serious criminal offense punishable by rigorous imprisonment.
panicSteps: Do not pay the bribe — paying bribes is also penalized under the law.
Note down the officer's name, badge number, station, time, and exact payment demands/QR code.
Call the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) Helpline immediately at 1064.
yourRights: You are legally protected from harassment when reporting corruption to the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) or CBI.
Demanding a bribe constitutes an offense under Section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

dos: Note down the officer's name, rank, police station, date, exact time, and the exact sum demanded.
Call the Anti-Corruption Helpline (1064) immediately to arrange a lawful trap operation.
Preserve any digital communication, WhatsApp chats, or payment QR codes requested.
donts: Do not pay the bribe. Paying bribes is also criminalized under the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act.

whereToComplain.action: Lodge immediate complaint for trap operation or investigation.
Report corruption involving central agencies or union territory personnel.

citations.description: Criminalizes public servants obtaining undue advantage.
Public servant disobeying direction under law to cause injury to any person.

scenarios.title: Threats, Abuse & Physical Assault
scenarios.quickSummary: Police brutality and verbal abuse violate Article 21. Stations are required to maintain functional CCTV cameras.
panicSteps: Prioritize safety first: call 112 if in danger, then go immediately to a government hospital casualty ward.
Demand a Medico-Legal Certificate (MLC) documenting all physical injuries.
Apply promptly to the Magistrate/SP to preserve police station CCTV footage.
yourRights: Supreme Court mandates operational CCTV cameras with night vision and audio across all police stations (Paramvir Singh Saini judgment).
Right to be free from custodial torture and dignity violations under Article 21.
Right to an independent medical examination (MLC) conducted at a government hospital.

dos: Go immediately to a government hospital casualty ward and request a Medico-Legal Certificate (MLC) detailing all injuries.
Take dated photographs and video documentation of physical marks or property damage.
File an application to preserve station CCTV footage before the overwrite window expires.
donts: Do not delay medical examination; prompt documentation is crucial for judicial evidence.

whereToComplain.action: File a complaint against serious misconduct, custodial violence, or extortion.
File a private criminal complaint under BNSS Sec. 223 / CrPC Sec. 200 against delinquent officers.
Lodge an urgent portal complaint for human rights violations and compensation.

citations.section: Paramvir Singh Saini v. Baljit Singh (2020)
citations.description: Mandatory CCTV in all police stations with 18-month storage directives.
Protection of life and personal liberty, including protection from custodial brutality.
